newsitem.title: USA: NYS general FY '97 fund balance higher - comptroller.
newsitem.headline: NYS general FY '97 fund balance higher - comptroller.

text.p: For the first half of New York State's fiscal 1997 year, which began April 1, the state's general fund had a balance of $665.8 million above forecast, the state comptroller reported Wednesday in the September cash report.
Receipts were $238.7 million above plan, spending was $596.7 million below plan and net transfers into the general fund were $169.6 million below plan, the comptroller reported.
State Comptroller H. Carl McCall said most of the spending variance was in local assistance.
"We are mid-way through the state's fiscal year and peformance so far looks good," McCall said in a statement. "Tax receipts collected are considerably higher than anticipated in the budget."

McCall attributed the "better-than-expected performance" to Wall Street's improved environment, which in turns spurs higher personal income tax estimated payments, growth in the bank tax and gains in the estate tax.
Through September for all governmental funds, tax collections totaled $17.6 billion, a 4.9 percent increase over the same period last year.

Personal income tax withholding is down 2.1 percent over the same period last year, because of tax reductions; estimated payments are up 16.5 percent and total personal income tax collections are up 6.7 percent to $9.0 billion.
Almost all of the increase this year in the personal income tax is from the size of last year's surplus, which counts as a collection this year, McCall said.
Sales tax is up 4.2 percent while total consumer taxes and fees are up 1.0 percent to $4.7 billion.
Business taxes are up 4.1 percent to $3.3 billion. Other taxes are up 7.4 percent to $498 million.
Miscellaneous receipts increased 1.5 percent to $4.1 billion. Federal funds increased 3.6 percent to $10.1 billion.
Disbursements for all governmental funds were done slightly, totaling $30.3 billion through September, McCall said.
McCall noted, "Surplus funds should not be an invitation to start a spending spree, but should be used to strengthen our finances."
McCall said the state has to deal with welfare reform and the potential for a slower economy and should use the surplus as an investment to deal with future problems.
